title: Bach's signature
hook: Bach signed his scores SDG, to God alone the glory

segments.voice: Yesterday, a friar with a brush, moving pollen between pea flowers. Your line was the monk's garden. What did you water, and did you leave it alone to grow? Day nine hundred ninety.

A church musician in Leipzig is up late, finishing a piece for Sunday. Choir parts, organ, strings, a hymn tune running through the middle of it all. He has a congregation to feed and a family to feed, and the deadline is days away, not months. He gets to the last bar, draws the final double line, and then, under the music, he writes three letters. S. D. G. Not his name. Not a date. Three letters, where a signature would go. His name was Johann Sebastian Bach. Today, Bach's signature.

S. D. G. stands for three Latin words: soli Deo gloria. To God alone the glory. It's a short way of saying that the credit for any good thing belongs to God, not to us. Bach was a Lutheran, and he wrote it at the end of scores. At the top of some, he wrote two other letters, J. J., for Jesu juva: Jesus, help. Help at the start, glory at the end. That's the whole shape of a working day in four letters. The idea has a long echo in scripture. The opening of Psalm 115, in the King James Bible: "Not unto us, O LORD, not unto us, but unto thy name give glory." Notice the psalmist says not unto us twice. It's hard to mean it the first time. And Paul takes the idea out of the church and into the kitchen: "Whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God." Eat, drink, whatever. Bach didn't save the letters for his grandest works. Tradition says he signed ordinary pieces too, written to a deadline for an ordinary Sunday. And some of his music for keyboard students, teaching pieces, carries a dedication along the same lines. The glory wasn't reserved for the masterpiece. It went on the homework. Bach could be stubborn, and he argued with his employers. The letters weren't a claim to be holy. They were a way of handing the work over when it was done.
screen: `SOLI DEO GLORIA: TO GOD ALONE THE GLORY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose one piece of work to sign. Settle, and breathe. Think through what's ahead of you today. An email. A meal. A shift. A report. A conversation with a child. Pick one ordinary thing. Now picture finishing it, and then, quietly, signing it, the way Bach signed his scores. If you pray, you can write or whisper the letters S. D. G. at the end of it, or say the psalm: not unto us, O Lord. If you don't, you can sign it for the person it serves, and let the credit go. Rest with that for the full two minutes. The bell holds the time.
Bach's signature. The letters S. D. G., soli Deo gloria, to God alone the glory, written by Johann Sebastian Bach at the end of his scores.
Your line: soli deo gloria. Today, finish the one thing you chose, and before you send it or serve it, sign it in your head with three small letters. Day nine hundred ninety.

howItsDone: Some Christian musicians, artists and writers still mark their work with S.D.G. or soli Deo gloria, and others dedicate their work to God in a short prayer before they begin.

trapdoor: what you thought: SDG is a composer's initials.
what it means: soli Deo gloria, to God alone the glory, written at the end of Bach's scores.
what a scholar hears: a Latin motto that echoes Psalm 115's not unto us, paired with J. J., Jesu juva, at the start: help at the beginning, glory at the end.

notes: Claims rule: no dates or counts of how many scores bear S.D.G.; 'at the end of scores' and 'at the top of some' kept general.
'Tradition says he signed ordinary pieces too' (weekly church cantatas); confirm.
'some of his music for keyboard students ... carries a dedication along the same lines': refers to the Orgelbüchlein title page ('to the highest God alone in honor'); confirm the paraphrase or cut.
Soli Deo gloria described as 'a Reformation watchword' without numbering the solas; confirm.
'Bach could be stubborn, and he argued with his employers': documented disputes with the Leipzig council and others; confirm wording is fair.
Hook scene (late night in Leipzig) is illustrative.
Editor pass: cut the unsourced 'Reformation watchword' claim from the teach and the trapdoor (trapdoor now ties the motto to Psalm 115); cut the stock line 'Here's what's striking about Bach.'
Second editor pass: hook simile 'the way you'd sign off a letter to someone you love' replaced with 'where a signature would go' (the love-letter image misdescribed the motto).

Audit pass: trapdoor no longer calls soli Deo gloria 'Psalm 115 in three Latin words' (the motto is not a translation of the psalm; the Latin psalm opens Non nobis, Domine); 'comes straight out of scripture' softened.
